pix/host._prod_loc_note: Then the daemon runtime: a third [[services]] runtime for a long-running HOST process that already speaks its own protocol on a loopback port. It exists because go-plugin is the wrong shape for one -- snow-proxy is reached over HTTP by an in-sandbox wrapper, so a net/rpc handshake would replace a working transport to gain nothing -- and because the Port/Listen/Health fields on Service were designed for exactly this and had no runtime that read them. It reuses everything that matters (staged copy-then-verify, env allowlist, restart budgets, the permanent-vs-transient split, and the rule that a running process is not health) and adds only launch + probe. The doctor row is the point: a pack daemon was the one host-exec facet with NO row, so when snow-proxy died the warehouse capability degraded in total silence. Then the third launch form. UnitSpec described only two ways to start a unit -- self-exec or a SHA-pinned external path -- so Validate rejected the one thing a pack daemon actually is: a binary the user built on their own Mac, which no shared manifest can carry a SHA for. The pack was accepted, the tree accepted the daemon, and then the unit it was handed could not describe itself, so snow-proxy never started and the failure surfaced only in a serve log. UnitSpec.Command closes that, joins identity() so a reattach cannot confuse two daemons, and is refused alongside a sha pin -- a pin naming a file the spec never reads is worse than no pin, because it reads as a guarantee. The consent screen renders it UNPINNED so the absence is the user's call, not a silent property.

pix/host/cli._prod_loc_note: 475 -> 502: Deps.Config() now warns about config keys this build ignores, so a typo is surfaced instead of silently doing nothing. A deliberate, reviewed raise of a shrink-only budget, which is the only way this number is allowed to move.

pix/host/cmd/pix._prod_loc_note: 3036 -> 3071: `pix resume SESSION [DIR]` turns pi's exact exit receipt into a host command without exposing `run -- --session`. Then 3071 -> 3136, edges 22 -> 23: `pix reset` is back (reset_cmd.go). The new edge is cmd/pix -> workflow/reset, and it is the whole point of the shape: reset is L3 and workflow/launch is its L3 sibling, so the command layer is the ONLY place allowed to hold both. It injects `pix rm --all` into reset as reset.Sweep rather than letting reset grow a sandbox removal of its own; that alternative would have cost no edge here and created a second bulk force-removal seam beside the one explicitly-named one. Deliberate, reviewed raises of a shrink-only budget. Then the independent-review round: three clean-slate reviewers attacked the first cut and found real gaps, all closed here. A pack's `probe` runs on the host and was in neither the fingerprint nor the consent screen, so a pack could change what pix executes without re-gating. `ActiveServerMCP` read only the LAST activated pack, so on a composed stack doctor accused half of it of being undeclared and recommended `sbx mcp rm` on servers it had just registered — and it read a pack that fails to load as a pack that declares nothing, which turned one manifest typo into that same advice for every server on the host. MCP names and probe argv[0] were the only pack identifiers not name-gated, while landing in commands users paste into a shell. `NonSecretEnvNames` excluded a secret per-integration rather than pack-wide, so one integration could allowlist another's credential into plaintext. Probes could outrun their budget with no WaitDelay, which matters precisely because they now run through `op run`. And doctor's own report said `✓ ready` over a row that had proved an integration unusable, undercounted the unknowns behind the gaps, and printed one repair when several were needed. Each fix is a few lines; the volume is that there were many, and every one was a way of claiming more than had been verified.

pix/host/config._prod_loc_note: prod_loc 796 -> 804: ServiceEnabled now resolves `services` the way `pix-host serve` does, and the load-bearing half is that EMPTY MEANS ALL (resolveServices: "an empty result means all"). A deliberate, reviewed raise.

pix/host/inference._prod_loc_note: raised together for ONE change: `pix doctor` and `pix setup` demanded an anthropic/openai/google key from hosts whose models need none. A pack's sbx-session backends carry their own credential (a Docker login session the sbx proxy injects inside the sandbox, unreplayable from the host by design), so the key store lists nothing and the required row went red prescribing `pix models add anthropic` -- a key nothing would read. `pix run`'s launch gate already skipped the key check on exactly this host (inference.ConfiguredKeylessInference); ProviderKeyProbe.Keyless + inference.KeylessBackends give the same carve-out to the two verbs that lacked it, so all three stop disagreeing about one host. Distinct from Callable, which answers "this key routes nowhere"; Keyless answers "no key was ever the credential". provision's new edge is importing inference for that one predicate rather than re-deriving a second opinion. A deliberate, reviewed raise of a shrink-only budget.

pix/host/service._prod_loc_note: 1664 -> 1708: `serve stop` now sweeps for orphaned `pix-host serve` processes AFTER stopping the pid its pidfile recorded. A pidfile names one daemon and is not proof there is only one, so a second daemon outliving its own pidfile kept holding :11435 while stop reported success. That is why `pix serve stop` had to be run twice. The sweep only ever signals pids that positively verify as our live serve. A deliberate, reviewed raise of a shrink-only budget. Then reset's post-stop settle: a launchd boot-out returns when the unit is unloaded, not when the process has exited, and this daemon closes a sqlite writer and reaps a supervised child on the way out. Two seconds was not enough on a real machine, so reset refused to move the data directory and left a HALF reset (config moved aside, data and state kept, every MCP registration removed) for a pid that was gone moments later. Then 1722 -> 1724: `pix serve` help described only memory, though serve now supervises the daemons a pack declares in [[services]]. Help that undersells what a command does is the same defect as help that oversells it -- a user onboarding today cannot find out that their pack's daemon is supervised here. `serve status` was verified to actually list those units before the help was allowed to claim it does.

It reuses everything that matters (staged copy-then-verify, env allowlist, restart budgets, the permanent-vs-transient split, and the rule that a running process is not health) and adds only launch + probe. The consent screen renders it UNPINNED so the absence is the user's call, not a silent property. And the startup budget. waitHealthy took HealthTimeout, the per-probe budget, for a daemon's FIRST health check -- so snow-proxy (~1.5s warm, ~3.5s cold) lost a coin flip against 3s, and a lost flip removes the unit from the tree, which a first-run user meets as a dead warehouse. Handshake already meant exactly 'how long may a unit take to become usable', so it now covers both unit kinds rather than growing a fourth timeout, and AddDaemon's outer wait derives from the same budget instead of firing while the inner poll is still legitimately running. The added lines are that comment plus countTrue; the launch path itself did not grow. Then hostpath.go, prod_loc 1703 -> 1815 and globals 29 -> 30 (errCommandNotFound). 'Resolved on PATH at launch' meant nothing in the environment that actually launches serve: launchd hands a login service PATH=/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin, and every host binary in this system lives elsewhere -- snow-proxy and slack-mcp in ~/.local/bin, snow and gog and op under Homebrew. So the daemon resolved perfectly in a developer's shell and failed PERMANENTLY under the managed service, which is the only way real users run it, while the error said 'is not on PATH' to someone whose interactive PATH did have it. The same gap hit the child: a daemon inheriting launchd's PATH starts, binds, and answers its health check while being unable to find the vendor CLI it shells out to -- every row green, capability broken, which is the defect class this whole release was about. Resolution now searches PATH then three code-pinned directories, the error names every one of them, and a unit that allowed PATH gets the same list so it can find its own tools. The list is pinned in code, not config: a manifest that could extend it could point `command` anywhere while keeping the same name on the consent screen. Then 1815 -> 1825: a daemon never recorded its probe latency, so `pix serve status` printed probe=0us for an HTTP GET over a socket. Zero reads as 'instant', not as 'never measured', and the latency of the probe that timed out is the number that explains the eviction after it -- which is why the go-plugin unit has always timed every probe, failures included. Now both kinds do.

Then the adversarial-verification round: a probe was wrapped in op run based on the SERVER's credentials rather than the probe's own needs, so BambooHR's credential-free 'docker image inspect' inherited a 1Password dependency it never had — turning a millisecond answer into 'not checkable' on a locked vault, and making a read-only diagnostic provoke an authorization prompt. It is wrapped now only when the probe invokes the server's own binary. And 'pix pack use' swallowed a registration failure into a note and exited 0, so adopting a pack on a machine missing one of its commands reported success for servers it had not registered. Then the first REAL pix setup run, which exposed what four review rounds could not because no agent was allowed to run that verb: the credential solicitor skipped every integration with a setup hook -- which is every integration that needs a credential -- so nothing was ever asked for and setup died on the first missing reference having offered no way to supply it. Credentials are now solicited BEFORE registration too, because registering first produced a bare, unwrapped server on a clean machine: exactly the broken state this whole surface exists to prevent. Requirements report all at once with pack-authored guidance, and a failed setup phase can no longer be headlined ready. Then the daemon runtime: a third [[services]] runtime for a long-running HOST process that already speaks its own protocol on a loopback port. It exists because go-plugin is the wrong shape for one -- snow-proxy is reached over HTTP by an in-sandbox wrapper, so a net/rpc handshake would replace a working transport to gain nothing -- and because the Port/Listen/Health fields on Service were designed for exactly this and had no runtime that read them. It reuses everything that matters (staged copy-then-verify, env allowlist, restart budgets, the permanent-vs-transient split, and the rule that a running process is not health) and adds only launch + probe. The doctor row is the point: a pack daemon was the one host-exec facet with NO row, so when snow-proxy died the warehouse capability degraded in total silence. Then 3363 -> 3408: setup's pack adopter passed interactive=false as a hardcoded constant, so a step whose remediation needs a terminal was refused on a run that had just prompted the user for a y/N and two 1Password references -- and the refusal told them to re-run without --yes/--non-interactive, flags they had never passed. The cost fell entirely on NEW users, which is why four review rounds missed it: a new user has no Slack grant by definition, so that step could never pass, its fix could never run, and `pix setup --pack` could never complete. Interactivity is measured now (setupInteractivity: !assumeYes && a real TTY, both load-bearing -- TTY alone would let --yes open a browser, --yes alone would prompt into a pipe), extracted into a function precisely because nothing could observe a constant. Also reasonBlock: a check's reason is a multi-line report carrying the pack's own guidance, and interpolated into a parenthetical it produced an eight-line sentence with the closing paren stranded at the end. It is a block under its heading, and absent entirely for an executable hook, which reports no reason at all. Then 3408 -> 3849, trustsummary.go: the consent screen was about seventy lines for a real pack, and Mark read one as a new user -- 'my god this is an overwhelming wall of text'. That is not cosmetic: a consent screen nobody reads is not consent, so length was costing the gate the thing it exists for. Most of it was REPETITION -- slack appeared once as a Host MCP with its health check and again as an Ensures: block with the same check plus a guidance paragraph -- and per-integration grouping scattered the one question a user has, what will execute on my machine, across the whole screen. The summary inverts it: counts, then ONE flat list of every command that runs here, which answers the security question better than the grouped view did. The detailed screen is unchanged and one keypress away (`d` at the prompt, or --details for a non-TTY review). The governing rule is tested: every fact the FINGERPRINT covers stays visible by DEFAULT, because a fact that re-gates while being invisible on the screen the user is re-asked on turns re-consent into a mystery prompt. That rule caught two of my own omissions mid-change -- remote URLs (host-only would have hidden a repointed path) and the env names that are not solicited credentials (GOG_ACCOUNT, literal EnvValues), both fingerprinted and both briefly dropped. Pack-authored HINTS are the one thing moved behind --details: prose, and prose cannot change what executes. Then 3849 -> 3912: the pack's guidance for a credential now prints AT the prompt that asks for it. Mark, after a successful run: 'i got asked for gog keyring password, but like how would a new user even get to that point as a prereq?' They would not have. The pack authors that guidance -- invent a passphrase, make a 1Password item, copy its secret reference -- and it rendered only on the adoption screen dozens of lines above the prompt, then behind the detail key once the screen was summarised. The text existed; the user never met it where it was actionable. Matched by env name, which the integration and the requirement already share, so a pack gets this by authoring one hint. Also: solicitPackCredentials RETURNED SILENTLY when the 1Password CLI was absent -- no prompt, no reason -- and the user then met a setup failure naming `pix secret set`, which also needs op. Every message pointed at a tool nothing had mentioned. It now says which references are needed and what to do, and deliberately does not prompt for a value it has nowhere to put.

pix/host/workflow/provision._prod_loc_note: raised together for ONE change: `pix doctor` and `pix setup` demanded an anthropic/openai/google key from hosts whose models need none. A pack's sbx-session backends carry their own credential (a Docker login session the sbx proxy injects inside the sandbox, unreplayable from the host by design), so the key store lists nothing and the required row went red prescribing `pix models add anthropic` -- a key nothing would read. `pix run`'s launch gate already skipped the key check on exactly this host (inference.ConfiguredKeylessInference); ProviderKeyProbe.Keyless + inference.KeylessBackends give the same carve-out to the two verbs that lacked it, so all three stop disagreeing about one host. Distinct from Callable, which answers "this key routes nowhere"; Keyless answers "no key was ever the credential". provision's new edge is importing inference for that one predicate rather than re-deriving a second opinion. A deliberate, reviewed raise of a shrink-only budget. Then the independent-review round: three clean-slate reviewers attacked the first cut and found real gaps, all closed here. A pack's `probe` runs on the host and was in neither the fingerprint nor the consent screen, so a pack could change what pix executes without re-gating. `ActiveServerMCP` read only the LAST activated pack, so on a composed stack doctor accused half of it of being undeclared and recommended `sbx mcp rm` on servers it had just registered — and it read a pack that fails to load as a pack that declares nothing, which turned one manifest typo into that same advice for every server on the host. MCP names and probe argv[0] were the only pack identifiers not name-gated, while landing in commands users paste into a shell. `NonSecretEnvNames` excluded a secret per-integration rather than pack-wide, so one integration could allowlist another's credential into plaintext. Probes could outrun their budget with no WaitDelay, which matters precisely because they now run through `op run`. And doctor's own report said `✓ ready` over a row that had proved an integration unusable, undercounted the unknowns behind the gaps, and printed one repair when several were needed. Each fix is a few lines; the volume is that there were many, and every one was a way of claiming more than had been verified. Then the first REAL pix setup run, which exposed what four review rounds could not because no agent was allowed to run that verb: the credential solicitor skipped every integration with a setup hook -- which is every integration that needs a credential -- so nothing was ever asked for and setup died on the first missing reference having offered no way to supply it. Credentials are now solicited BEFORE registration too, because registering first produced a bare, unwrapped server on a clean machine: exactly the broken state this whole surface exists to prevent. Requirements report all at once with pack-authored guidance, and a failed setup phase can no longer be headlined ready. Then 1321 -> 1346, Step.ProbeProvesSubset: the harness skipped any step whose first check passed, on the rule that a proven capability must not be touched. That rule assumed a probe verifies what its apply performs, and for `pack` it does not. PackProbe answers 'is a pack active'; the pack apply adopts the pack AND runs its required setup hooks. So on every host where the pack was already active -- which is every host after the first run -- `pix setup --pack X` skipped all of that pack's hooks and printed ready having checked none of its integrations. A user re-running setup to repair a broken integration got a no-op and a green screen, with nothing in the output to tell the difference. Measured on the real pack: four required steps, zero run before, four reporting ready after. The added lines are the field and the comment explaining when NOT to reach for it (prefer strengthening the probe; this is for the case where the probe cannot reasonably cover the apply, since covering it here would mean running every pack's host requirement checks inside every `pix doctor`). Then 1346 -> 1357: the report now names `pix doctor`. Setup grades only the capabilities it OWNS, which is correct -- it must not claim to have checked something it cannot install -- but the rows it leaves out (mcp, daemons, memory) are the ones that say whether the work functions. Setup can install a launchd agent, verify the agent is loaded, and be entirely right while a unit under it is dead. Before this, `✓ ready` was the last line a new user saw and nothing told them a fuller report existed. Then 1357 -> 1372: a pack failure was printed TWICE -- in full in the `failed` row, then again as the command's final error, since that wraps the same cause. Two copies of an eight-line paragraph read as two different problems. The row shows the first line with an ellipsis; the full block appears once, at the end, where the exit code points and where it is the last thing the user sees. The cause is still wrapped, so nothing is lost and errors.Is still works -- a test pins that the top-level error carries the pack's own refusal.

pix/host/workflow/reset._prod_loc_note: Then reset's post-stop settle: a launchd boot-out returns when the unit is unloaded, not when the process has exited, and this daemon closes a sqlite writer and reaps a supervised child on the way out. Two seconds was not enough on a real machine, so reset refused to move the data directory and left a HALF reset (config moved aside, data and state kept, every MCP registration removed) for a pid that was gone moments later.
